subject: Vocabulary
description: High-hit PYQ idioms across Clerk → UPSC levels

options.option_text: Very expensive
Extremely easy to do
A celebration
A small part of something

questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' — something trivially easy. 'The exam was a piece of cake.'
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: On a specific lunar day
Very rarely
At night only
Regularly

questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' = extremely seldom. A 'blue moon' (astronomy) is the second full moon in a calendar month — rare phenomenon.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'To burn the candle at both ends' means:

options.option_text: To waste resources
To exhaust oneself by working too hard
To be an efficient worker
To light a room with two candles

questions.explanation: A candle burned at both ends is used up twice as fast — meaning: overworking to exhaustion, sleeping too little, overextending oneself. especially late into the night.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

_fixes.was: To exhaust oneself by working too hard (especially late into the night)
_fixes.now: To exhaust oneself by working too hard

options.option_text: To complicate things further
To solve a difficult problem by a bold, decisive action
To untie a literal rope
To run away from a problem

questions.explanation: From the legend of Alexander the Great, who cut through the impossibly tangled Gordian knot with a sword rather than try to untie it. Means: solve something intractable by a decisive unconventional move.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'To add fuel to the fire' means:

options.option_text: To put out a disagreement
To worsen an already tense situation
To start a new business
To provide constructive criticism

questions.explanation: To do or say something that makes a bad situation worse. Metaphor of literally pouring oil on a fire to intensify it.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: To start a new activity
To give up / admit defeat
To wash thoroughly
To reward someone

questions.explanation: From boxing — a corner-man throwing a towel into the ring signals surrender on the fighter's behalf. Means: accept defeat, give up.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A crushing defeat that looks like a win
A win so costly that it is tantamount to defeat
A victory through cunning rather than force
A spectacular easy triumph

questions.explanation: After King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who defeated the Romans at Heraclea (280 BCE) and Asculum (279 BCE) at such heavy cost to his own forces that he famously said, 'If we win one more victory over the Romans, we shall be ruined.' Editorial favourite for writing about wars, election victories etc.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'To nip something in the bud' means:

options.option_text: To protect a plant
To stop (a problem) at an early stage before it develops
To prune something gently
To delay something indefinitely

questions.explanation: To 'nip' = pinch off. 'In the bud' = before flowering. Metaphor: stop an undesirable development before it grows.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to bite the bullet' mean?

options.option_text: to endure a painful or difficult situation with courage
to take revenge on a person who has wronged you first
to speak bluntly without considering the consequences
to make a hasty decision when under extreme pressure

questions.explanation: A is correct — the idiom originates from soldiers biting a bullet during surgery to endure pain without anaesthesia; figuratively it means facing hardship stoically. Option D is a common distractor because pressure is involved, but 'hasty decision under pressure' fits 'snap judgement', not this idiom.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to sit on the fence' mean?

options.option_text: to remain neutral and avoid taking either side in a dispute
to be excessively cautious while managing one's finances
to refuse to participate in any kind of group activities
to deliberately delay a firm decision until the very end

questions.explanation: A is correct — sitting on a fence (literally between two sides) captures deliberate neutrality in a controversy. Option D is tempting because both involve not deciding, but the idiom specifically denotes taking no side, not mere procrastination.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to beat around the bush' mean?

options.option_text: to avoid getting to the main point of a discussion
to exaggerate facts in order to impress other people
to look for something persistently in the wrong places
to spread unverified rumours without any factual basis

questions.explanation: A is correct — from hunting, where beaters would drive prey out by circling bushes rather than going straight to the quarry; figuratively it means talking around a subject without addressing it directly. Option B confuses this with 'draw the long bow', which implies exaggeration.

questions.stem: The idiom 'to spill the beans' is best used when someone:

options.option_text: squanders resources carelessly on trivial or minor issues
accidentally or carelessly discloses confidential information
loses composure and shows anger in a very public setting
creates confusion by mixing up important data or details

questions.explanation: B is correct — 'spill the beans' means to let out a secret, usually inadvertently. Option C is a plausible distractor because both involve loss of control, but losing temper publicly is covered by idioms like 'fly off the handle', not this one.

questions.stem: When someone is said to have 'got the upper hand', it means they have:

options.option_text: completed an important task well ahead of the deadline
demanded a larger share of profits than they deserve
gained a position of control or advantage over another party
received formal credit for work actually done by someone else

questions.explanation: C is correct — 'the upper hand' evokes a dominant grip position in wrestling or swordplay, signifying control over another. Option A is wrong; completing work early means 'getting ahead', not gaining power over a rival or opponent.

questions.stem: The idiom 'to play second fiddle' describes a person who:

options.option_text: performs assigned duties without full effort or real commitment
actively attempts to outshine the person they are supporting
extends support to someone undeserving of their current position
occupies a subordinate or secondary role relative to another person

questions.explanation: D is correct — in an orchestra the second violin section supports and follows the first (lead) violin; figuratively the idiom means playing a lesser, supporting role to someone else. Option A (half-hearted work) is captured by 'going through the motions', not this idiom.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates the idiom 'carrying coals to Newcastle'?

options.option_text: Sending an IT expert to teach coding skills to experienced software developers
Dispatching emergency food supplies to a drought-stricken region in great need
Explaining constitutional amendments to first-year law students in college
Organising a road-safety workshop for a group of newly licensed taxi drivers

questions.explanation: A is correct — Newcastle upon Tyne was England's premier coal-mining centre; bringing coal there is a pointless surplus. Teaching advanced coding to expert developers is equally redundant. Options C and D involve imparting knowledge to people who genuinely lack it, which is purposeful rather than superfluous.
